opus-5.5.text:
I'm fairly skeptical that we'll get a clean one-to-one mapping, and I think it's worth being precise about why.

The appeal of sparse autoencoders is obvious. You take a model's activations, which are dense and hard to read, and decompose them into a much larger set of features where only a few are active at a time. Then you look at what makes each feature fire and give it a label: "this is the Golden Gate Bridge feature," "this is the deception feature." It feels like a dictionary between the model's internal language and ours.

But a few things make me cautious.

First, there's no guarantee the model carves up the world the way we do. Natural language concepts are the product of human history, culture, and what was useful for people to talk about. A neural network trained to predict text may find a completely different basis useful. Some of its features may be blends of several human concepts, and some human concepts may be spread across many features. When we label a feature, we're often projecting a neat word onto something messier.

Second, the decomposition isn't unique. If you train SAEs of different sizes, features split and merge. A "dog" feature at one size becomes "dog in a photo," "dog as a pet," and "the word dog" at a larger size. So which one is the model's real concept? That suggests the features are partly an artifact of our method, not a ground truth we've uncovered.

Third, and this is what I care about most, is the gap between correlation and causation. A feature that fires on certain inputs isn't necessarily what the model *uses* to compute its output. When my collaborators and I have benchmarked these methods on practical tasks, like steering a model toward a concept or detecting whether a concept is present, SAEs often don't beat much simpler baselines. Sometimes just prompting the model, or training a simple linear probe, works as well or better. That's a sign that the nice-looking dictionary isn't capturing the causally relevant structure as cleanly as we'd hope.

So my view is that natural language is a useful *interface* for describing what's going on inside models, but I don't expect a one-to-one correspondence. The more productive framing, I think, is causal: rather than asking "what does this feature mean?", ask "if I intervene on this part of the model, does its behavior change in the way my hypothesis predicts?" That's a higher bar, but it tells you whether your explanation is actually faithful to the model, rather than just a story that sounds right.

I don't want to be dismissive. SAEs have been a great tool for generating hypotheses and they've surfaced interesting structure. I just think we should treat them as a starting point for investigation and not as a finished translation of the model's mind into English.

r002.rationale: It describes SAEs as hypothesis-generating starting points, says they may miss causally relevant structure, and calls for causal intervention to establish faithful explanations—indicating these translation methods are insufficient on their own for interpretability.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm pretty skeptical of a clean one-to-one mapping, honestly. Sparse autoencoders are a genuinely useful tool, but the picture they give you is a lot messier than the "dictionary of concepts" framing suggests.

A few reasons. First, the features you get out of an SAE are heavily dependent on your choices: the dictionary size, the sparsity penalty, which layer you train on, the data distribution. Train two SAEs with different widths on the same activations and you'll get features that split and merge in ways that don't look like there's a single canonical set of concepts underneath. That "feature splitting" phenomenon is really telling. If there were a privileged basis of natural-language concepts, you'd expect it to be more stable than it is.

Second, interpretability of a feature is often in the eye of the beholder. You look at the top activating examples, you write a label, and it feels right. But when people have actually tested whether those labels predict activations on held-out data, or whether steering with the feature does what the label says it should, the results are mixed. A lot of features are polysemantic in subtle ways, or they're tracking something about the input that doesn't correspond to a word we'd naturally use.

Third, and this is the deeper point, there's no particular reason the model's internal ontology should line up with human linguistic categories at all. The model is optimized to predict text, not to carve the world at the same joints we do. Some of its representations will be legible because language itself is structured around concepts we care about. But others will be weird compressions or computational conveniences that don't have a short English description.

So where I land is that SAEs give you a partial, lossy, somewhat arbitrary decomposition that's still very practically useful. You can find features that are faithful enough to do causal interventions, to debug behavior, to steer. That's a big deal. But I'd frame the goal less as "translate the model into English" and more as "find a description language that's good enough for the specific question you're asking." The one-to-one dream assumes a kind of structure that I don't think the evidence supports, and I'd rather we build evaluation methods that measure how faithful and how useful our explanations actually are, rather than taking the interpretability at face value.

r002.rationale: It describes SAEs as a partial, lossy decomposition and says translating the model into English is not the right general goal, indicating these methods are insufficient to solve all interpretability problems.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical that there’s a one-to-one correspondence. Natural language is one way of describing what a model represents, but there’s no particular reason its internal representations should line up neatly with concepts we have words for.

A sparse autoencoder tries to decompose activations into features that are sparsely active. Some of those features may have a recognizable interpretation, and we can give them a label. But the label is a hypothesis about the feature, not a complete description of it. A feature we call “deception,” for example, might respond to several related patterns that our label doesn’t distinguish.

There’s also a distinction between finding a feature that correlates with something and showing that the model actually uses it in the way we think. You’d want to intervene on that feature and see whether the resulting behavior matches your prediction across different contexts.

So I think sparse autoencoders can be useful for understanding models without giving us a perfect translation into English. The goal I’d put more weight on is an explanation that lets us predict and test what the model does, rather than assigning every internal feature a natural-language name.

r001.rationale: The response expresses skepticism about a one-to-one correspondence and gives reasons it may not hold; it does not affirm that such a correspondence could exist in principle.

r002.rationale: It says sparse autoencoders can help without providing a perfect English translation, and favors explanations that predict and test behavior, communicating that natural-language translation alone is insufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about expecting a one-to-one correspondence. Natural language is one way we describe concepts, but there’s no particular reason a model’s internal representations have to divide the world along exactly the same boundaries as our words.

Sparse autoencoders give us a way to look for features within those representations. Some features may have a fairly intuitive description, but being able to attach a label to a feature doesn’t mean that label captures everything the feature does. And a concept we express with one word might involve several features, depending on context.

So I’d distinguish finding useful, interpretable structure from finding an exact translation into language. The former seems plausible and valuable; the latter is a much stronger claim. Ideally, we’d test an interpretation by intervening on the feature and checking whether the model’s behavior changes in the way we predict, rather than relying only on how convincing its natural-language description sounds.
